title: The seventh-day sacrifice
hook: a week-old baby, a sheep, and a meal shared in thanks

segments.voice: Yesterday, the naming, and your line: a good name. Did you find out what your name means? Yesterday's seventh-day report named other things done that day. Here is one. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

Seven days after a birth, the backyard fills up. Pots the size of laundry baskets. Rice, meat, aunties arguing happily about salt. Neighbors who've never met the baby carrying plates home. Somewhere in the middle of it, a tired mother and father, and a week-old child sleeping through the whole thing. The meat on those plates comes from a sheep slaughtered in thanks for this one small person. That slaughter has a name: the 'aqiqah. Today: what it is, where it comes from, and why it's a meal for everyone.
screen: `A BACKYARD, A WEEK AFTER BIRTH.` → `PLATES GOING HOME.` → `A SHEEP, IN THANKS.`

segments.voice: First, the words. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Salman ibn 'Amir reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in paraphrase: with the boy there is an 'aqiqah, so shed blood on his behalf, and remove harm from him. That second half belongs to tomorrow. Today, the first: blood shed for a child, as an act of thanks. Second, the day. Samurah reports, in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi, in paraphrase: every boy is held in pledge by his 'aqiqah, which is slaughtered for him on the seventh day. Held in pledge is a striking phrase, and its meaning is discussed. Some readers hear it as a debt of thanks that belongs to the child's arrival. Third, girls and boys. Umm Kurz reports, in Abu Dawud, in paraphrase: for a boy, two sheep that are alike, and for a girl, one. So the 'aqiqah is for daughters as well as sons. How strongly it's urged, and the details of day and number, are questions families take to their own scholars, and they follow their means. Fourth, the meal. Tradition says the 'aqiqah isn't eaten alone: it's cooked, shared with relatives and neighbors, and part is given to people in need. A week after a birth, when a new family could easily close the door and sleep, the custom opens the door and sets out plates. A child's arrival becomes good news for the street. Thanks, in the 'aqiqah, isn't only said. It's served.
screen: `WITH THE BOY, AN 'AQIQAH.` · `HELD IN PLEDGE, THE SEVENTH DAY.` · `FOR DAUGHTERS AND FOR SONS.` · `THANKS SERVED ON PLATES.`

segments.voice: The practice: share food for a child's birth. Settle, and breathe. Think of a child whose birth you're glad of. A new baby you know. A niece or nephew. Your own child. Or, if it fits, the day you were born, and whoever was glad of you. Hold that gladness a moment. Then plan one small share of food in that child's name: a plate taken next door, a meal paid for someone, a box of sweets brought to work. If you pray, you can thank Allah for that child by name. The bell holds the time.
'Aqiqah. The sacrifice for a newborn, on the seventh day in Samurah's report, for daughters and sons, its meat shared with family, neighbors and those in need. Today's word.
Your line: thanks for a child. Today, share something to eat in the name of a child you're glad exists, and tell someone why. Tomorrow, shaving the hair. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Muslim families who hold the 'aqiqah slaughter a sheep or goat for a newborn, traditionally on the seventh day, and share the meat with relatives, neighbors and people in need, following their own scholars on how strongly it is urged.
